item.content:encoded:
I like it (in fact, it's a bit frustrating because I had a very similar idea for an SPC. :P Oh well, I suppose it's still different enough that I can submit it eventually anyway) but I do have a few problems with it:

+ show block
– hide block

Mainly I feel that the article has too many unnecessary details. The whole part on testing protocol especially feels bloated. I can see having a little bit of stuff like that to give the article a more clinical and professional feel as well as add to the lore but it feels a lot of it could be cut without really losing anything.

It doesn't help that I found the whole thing about the supercomputer giving a vague description of the text or pictures to be rather silly. It comes off as the equivalent of the "enhance button" in bad TV shows to me.

And in general, I feel like it could be re-worded more simply to make it a smoother read. For example, this passage:

SCP-592 is a large hardcover book which exhibits no external qualities that could be considered unusual, but which can cause delusions, psychosis, changes in physical health and appearance, or even severe wounding when read.

Why bother specifying that it shows no external abnormal quality? The fact that you said the effects occur when someone reads the book already implies that there are otherwise no anomalous effects. You could say just as much in fewer words by saying "SCP-592 is a large hardcover book which can cause mental issues and physical alterations when read".

There are also a few spots that confuse me. In the containment procedures, it says:

The front and back covers of SCP-592 are to be covered in black opaque tape at all times.

I'm not sure why that's necessary as looking at the covers would not cause the effects to ocur, would it? It's even more confusing when later it says that the spine is uncovered, which seems to confirm this.

at some point no later than 15 June 1956, a date researchers have termed the Point of Divergence (PoD), the text begins to diverge from known history.

Shouldn't the point of divergence be more specific than "no later" than a certain date? It seems like it would be easy for the Foundation to verify that information.


Please collapse long posts. ~Zyn

Anyway, nitpicking aside, like I said, I do like this entry. I just feel it could be even better with a little bit more polish.

item.content:encoded:
After reading this discussion page, I guess I understand why this article is so highly rated…but I'm still giving it a neutral vote. I realize some things have been added to the cliche to make it a cliche that's "done well", but I feel like I've read enough similar things here that it's not unique or original enough to hook me.

What really got me to facepalm, though, was when the D-Class got a scar on his [blacked out FIVE LETTER WORD]. I can only think of three potential five-letter-word body parts that are visible from the outside, and I guess it could be "scalp" or "thumb", but the fact that the Foundation went to the trouble of asking his WIFE about it, considering how highly they prioritize security and secrecy…yeah. Maybe I'm just being nit-picky and humorless, which I guess is my own problem and not a problem with the article, but the fact that I facepalmed while reading this still clinches my neutral vote. I might still give it a neutral vote anyway, but this makes me decisive about it.

Sorry if I offended anyone.

The whole computer analysis thing is unnecessary unless the SCP has a memetic effect. If the SCP isn't memetic then you can just have a D-class read it out loud. If that would trigger the effect, then instead give the D-class a bunch of history books, and say "These are fake history books. Read them and tell us what in them is fake and why it's fake". Do this with multiple times with different people, compare the results to weed out lies and misunderstandings, and you'll get a lot more information than the computer would give you.

On the other hand, if it is memetic, then the "Church of the True History" wouldn't have been controversial, since they would have converted everyone they talked to.
